parsed_answer.content: Method reference syntax, denoted by the double-colon (::) operator, was introduced in Java 8 as a syntactic sugar to make functional interfaces more concise and readable. It serves as a shorthand for lambda expressions that simply call an existing method. By using a method reference, you are essentially passing a pointer to an existing method implementation as an argument, rather than defining a new lambda body that invokes that method. This reduces boilerplate code and improves clarity, especially when dealing with the Stream API or event handling, by transforming verbose functional logic into a declarative, intent-focused style.

items: The compiler performs a type inference check against the target functional interface's abstract method signature to ensure the method reference is compatible.
Unbound instance method references (e.g., String::length) work because the first parameter of the functional interface is treated as the target object (the 'this' context) for the method call.

Method references do not create a new scope; they simply reference an existing method, which can lead to slightly better performance in some JIT scenarios by avoiding the creation of an extra stack frame for the lambda body.
Constructor references (ClassName::new) allow you to treat class instantiation as a factory function, which is highly useful for dependency injection or collection initialization.

parsed_answer.content: A common 'senior' pitfall is over-using method references when the logic is not immediately obvious. While 'ClassName::method' is clean, it can obscure the actual arguments being passed if the functional interface has a complex signature. Furthermore, if you use a method reference on an object that is null at runtime, you will trigger a NullPointerException immediately upon invocation, whereas a lambda might have allowed for a null-safe check inside the block.
